author: Claude C. Hopkins
biz: Give your own purity a meaning

Your HomeownersLoan and Apply4Loan pages almost certainly lean on words like trusted, expert and experienced. Those are brewers crying pure. This week take your three strongest claims and replace each with a specific you can actually evidence: how many lenders sit on the panel, your median time from enquiry to a decision in principle, and exactly when and how the broker fee is disclosed. No approval or rate promises, nothing you cannot show a file for. Then measure, by ad group against the previous four weeks, the share of enquiries reaching a suitable completed application, and your complaint rate.
Ask for nothing on the first approach

At Debt Support Direct the caller is often frightened, so Hopkins's rule and the Consumer Duty point the same way: offer service, do not push. Replace the loudest call to action on the main entry page with something useful on its own, a plain comparison of the realistic options and what each one actually costs and risks, readable without handing over a phone number. Then track two numbers weekly: the proportion of enquiries where the notes show the client reached an informed decision, and the cost per customer who ends up with a suitable outcome, split by traffic source. Cut the sources that deliver neither.

b: Claude Clarence Hopkins was born on the twenty fourth of April 1866 in Hillsdale, Michigan, into a family with a long line of clergymen behind it and almost no money in it. His mother was a Scotch woman and a college graduate, and when she was left to raise her children alone she kept them alive by teaching school. She did the housework before the morning bell and again after it, wrote kindergarten books in the evenings, and in the holidays travelled from schoolhouse to schoolhouse selling them herself.

Religion in that house was not comfort, it was weather. His grandfather was a Hardshell Baptist and his mother a Scotch Presbyterian, and between them, Hopkins wrote, they made religion oppressive. Sundays meant five services and no walking for pleasure. He was allowed the Bible and a Concordance, though he smuggled in Pilgrim's Progress. Dancing, cards, the theatre and any book that was not a Sunday school book were all counted as sin.

From the age of nine he paid his own way. Before school he opened and warmed two schoolhouses and dusted the seats, and after school he swept them. He carried the Detroit Evening News to sixty five homes. On Saturdays he cleaned the schoolhouses and handed out bills, and on Sundays he was the church janitor. In the holidays he worked on a farm, and when a doctor decided he was too sickly for school he went into a cedar swamp to cut poles and hew railway ties.

Two things came out of that childhood and never left him. Poverty, he said, taught him about ordinary people, what they want and what they can afford to want. And he had watched his mother carry a product from door to door and count what came back, which is the whole of direct response advertising in one tired woman with a bag of books.

One warning belongs here. Hopkins wrote that his father died. Researchers who later went through the local records found evidence that his father deserted the family instead. The very first fact in this life is already in dispute, which is worth knowing about the man who taught the world to demand evidence.

b: He was being prepared for the ministry, and he was good at it. He preached his first sermon at seventeen. At eighteen he stood up in a Chicago pulpit with his mother sitting in the congregation.
What he said from that pulpit was that there was no hell fire, and that the story of Jonah and the whale would not survive examination. He called it afterwards the most daring event of my life.

Nobody shouted at him. That was the terrible part. In his words, the audience filed out in silence, and not a man or woman came to greet me. A few days later, at a lunch on Dearborn Street, his mother told him that he no longer was her son. He got up, walked out, and the door to a clergyman's life closed behind him.

He kept the trade, though, all of it. A preacher's job is to move strangers with words and then take a collection. What Hopkins had lost was the willingness to assert things he could not check. He had been raised to believe without evidence and he had just discovered that he could not do it.

Advertising, when he found his way to it, was a pulpit with a cash register at the back. You could say your piece to thousands of strangers, and then, unlike any preacher in history, you could count exactly how many of them believed you.

b: He went to a commercial school in Grand Rapids and joined the Bissell Carpet Sweeper Company in February as assistant bookkeeper at forty dollars a month. By November he was head bookkeeper at seventy five, good with figures and bored out of his mind.

So he started writing to dealers. For Christmas he offered the carpet sweeper not as a household tool but as a present, with display racks and cards that read The Queen of Christmas Presents, and he made the dealers sign an agreement to actually display them. He sent about five thousand letters. In his words, they brought me one thousand orders, almost the first orders we had ever received by mail.

Then he pushed the company to make the sweeper in twelve different woods, so that a buyer could match the furniture, and sold two hundred and fifty thousand of them in three weeks. That Christmas promotion ran in nearly two dozen magazines and over a thousand newspapers.

The sweeper matters less than the post bag. A letter that goes out on Monday brings an order on Thursday or it brings nothing, and either way you know. One offer can be set against another and the argument settled by counting envelopes. Hopkins had found a machine for turning opinions into facts, and he never worked any other way again.

A caution again. Scholars who went through Bissell's own surviving records put this breakthrough in 1890 and could not confirm every figure he gave. He was writing from memory nearly forty years later, and memory is a flatterer.

b: Swift and Company hired him at the Chicago stockyards to sell Cotosuet, a cooking fat competing with Cottolene from N. K. Fairbank. His version cost half a cent a pound more than the rival, and bakers would not touch it.

Rothschild and Company were opening a new store in Chicago. I will build there, Hopkins said, the largest cake in the world. It was baked by H. H. Kohlsaat and Company using Cotosuet instead of butter, and the crowds were so heavy that the police closed the doors to control them. In one week a hundred and five thousand people climbed four flights of stairs to look at a cake. He took the stunt to cities in the east and to a public market in Cleveland.

Boston was the harder problem. The branch there cost two thousand dollars a month and its six salesmen had sold almost nothing to bakers. Hopkins went to the largest baker in the district, the Fox Pie Company of Chelsea, and offered something no salesman had offered: a pie card, free advertising for the baker's own pies, in exchange for Cotosuet orders. The first thousand cards sold four carloads. In Springfield a baker named Teddy Mansfield took two carloads, and Hopkins had the railway cars themselves lettered with signs on both sides.

His conclusion was blunt. Real salesmanship, he wrote, has no regard for price. Nobody buys cheapness, they buy what they want, and what a baker wants is customers. Give him those and the half penny stops being the conversation.
ch.cap: Crowds climb four flights to see a cake

b: He spent six and one half years in Racine, Wisconsin, working for Dr Shoop's patent medicine company. Office hours began at seven o'clock in the morning.

Shoop had a specific problem. He was selling medicines through agents, Hopkins wrote, and he had no drug store trade. The agents were failing and the chemists' shelves were shut to him. A guarantee was the obvious answer, and guarantees were already everywhere and worth nothing, because they were signed by a company in another state that the customer would never meet.

So Hopkins moved the signature. I conceived the idea, he wrote, of having a neighborhood druggist, to whom people paid their money, sign the guaranty. Take the bottle home. If it does not help you, the man down the road whose face you have known for years will hand your money back. He tried it first on a cough cure and reported that it brought enormous results, then ran the same plan on Dr Shoop's Restorative and his Rheumatic Cure. He kept local accounts going at the same time, Racine Incubators and the Racine Shoe Company among them.

The mechanism is worth owning because it has not aged a day. Reverse the risk, and borrow trust you have not yet earned from somebody who has already earned it. Every free trial and every money back promise since is a version of that.

And then the honesty. These were nostrums, bottles sold on claims nobody could support. When Hopkins came to write about those years he opened the chapter like a man in the dock: now I come to a class of advertising of which I no longer approve. The method was sound. The product was not. He is the best witness against himself that we have.
ch.cap: The local chemist signs the guarantee

b: Schlitz was in fifth place. Every brewer in America, Hopkins noted, was at that time crying Pure, in letters a foot high, and the word had been shouted so often that it had stopped carrying anything at all.

He went to Milwaukee and asked to be shown round. They showed him plate glass rooms where the beer was cooled in filtered air. Great filters filled with white wood pulp. Every pump and pipe cleaned twice daily to avoid contamination. Every bottle cleaned four times by machinery. Artesian wells sunk four thousand feet for pure water, by a brewery that stood on the shore of Lake Michigan. Vats where the beer was aged six months before it went out to the drinker. And in the laboratory, under glass, the original mother yeast cell, developed through twelve hundred experiments to bring out the utmost in flavour, from which every drop of Schlitz yeast had been grown.

His guide was almost apologetic about it. Every good brewer did much the same thing. That, Hopkins realised, was exactly why it would work: a story common to the whole trade and never once told. He put the plate glass, the wells, the four washings and the twelve hundred experiments into print, and in his own summary of what he had done, I gave purity a meaning.

Schlitz, he wrote, jumped from fifth place to neck and neck with first place in a very few months. Cyrus Curtis, the publisher, who had never drunk beer in his life, read one of the advertisements and ordered a bottle.
Years later he compressed the lesson into six words that should be pinned above every marketing desk. No generality has any weight whatever.

b: In 1907, at forty one, Albert Lasker brought Hopkins into Lord and Thomas in Chicago. David Ogilvy later reported the salary as a hundred and eighty five thousand dollars a year, which would have made him the best paid writer in America by a wide margin. The figure is repeated everywhere and rests on thin sourcing, so hold it loosely.

Walking through a Quaker mill with Lasker, the two of them watched grain being fired out of steel guns under pressure to puff it up. Hopkins had the product called Wheat Berries renamed Puffed Wheat, so that it and Puffed Rice could be sold together, and wrote the line that carried both: food shot from guns.

The trade thought he had lost his mind. One paper called it the theory of an imbecile. Nobody, he was told, will eat something advertised as ammunition. Puffed Wheat and Puffed Rice went on to become the two most profitable cereals in the country, with sales of both rising three hundred per cent.

The work that mattered more, though, was quieter. He put coupons in advertisements and keyed each one, so that a returning slip of paper told him which newspaper and which headline had produced it. One advertisement for Van Camp evaporated milk brought back more than one million four hundred and sixty thousand coupons. For Van Camp's pork and beans he reported that they were baked for hours at two hundred and forty five degrees, because a number is a fact and delicious is not.
Out of all that counting came the sentence that is the whole of his method. Almost any question can be answered, cheaply, quickly and finally, by a test campaign.

b: Pepsodent came to him through an old friend and he turned it down flat. He did not see a way, he said, to educate the laity in technical tooth paste theories. Then he changed his mind on one condition: a six month option on a block of the company's stock. It was the wisest financial decision of his life.

Reading dental textbooks he found a passing reference to mucin plaques. He called it the film, and wrote the line that did all the work. Just run your tongue across your teeth. Anyone could do that in a second and feel something unpleasant they had never named. The reward he offered was not health but beauty: why would any woman carry dingy film on her teeth when Pepsodent takes it off.

The numbers are extraordinary. Before the campaign about seven Americans in a hundred kept toothpaste in the house. Ten years after it went national, sixty five in a hundred did. Brushing became something more than half a country did every day, and by the end of the second war the army had stopped treating recruits' mouths as a crisis.

Here is where later research takes the book apart. Charles Duhigg, among others, points out that the film is a natural membrane that forms on everyone's teeth whatever they eat, that brushing does not remove it, and that rival brands had used almost exactly the same words about film and beauty and got nowhere. What actually hooked people, on that account, was the tingle, the citric acid and the oil of mint, a sensation they began to miss on the nights they skipped.

If that is right, the most carefully measured advertising man who ever lived sold a feeling while believing he was selling a fact. His numbers were honest and his explanation was wrong. Hold that next to everything else in this story.

b: He finished at Lord and Thomas as its president and chairman, and by 1927 the agency was second only to J. Walter Thompson in total billings. Then he retired, and in 1923 he sat down and set the whole method out in about twenty thousand words.

Scientific Advertising opens without any throat clearing at all. Advertising is salesmanship. Its principles are the principles of salesmanship. And a line later: the only purpose of advertising is to make sales. Not awareness, not reputation, not the warm feeling of having been seen.

From there the rules come fast. Be specific, because no generality has any weight whatever. Offer something rather than demand something, because the best ads ask no one to buy. Keep the funny costume off, because people do not patronize a clown. And when two clever people disagree, stop arguing: almost any question can be answered, cheaply, quickly and finally, by a test campaign.

What holds it together is arithmetic. A headline is not good because the room liked it at the meeting. It is good because it brought customers at a lower cost per customer than the other headline, across a sample large enough to trust. So our final conclusions, he wrote, are always based on cost per customer or cost per dollar of sale, and mail order advertising is traced down to the fraction of a penny.
He never sold the book. Lord and Thomas gave it away. It is still, a hundred years on, the shortest useful education in the subject.

b: My Life in Advertising was serialised in Advertising and Selling and then published in book form by Harper in 1927. Hopkins died in September 1932 at Spring Lake, Michigan, at sixty six. He was elected to the Advertising Hall of Fame in 1957, twenty five years after his death.

David Ogilvy, who built his own career on the book, wrote the sentence that keeps it in print. Nobody should be allowed to have anything to do with advertising until he has read this book seven times.

The irony is almost too neat. A boy raised to believe without evidence built a career on refusing to, and then wrote a memoir that his own paper trail partly contradicts. The dates drift. The figures are generous. His father, by the records, may have walked out rather than died. The honest way to read him is the way he taught: respect the method, check the claims, including his.

What survives him is a short list and it is still the best one going. Test rather than argue. Be specific rather than impressive. Offer service rather than ask for the order. Judge everything by cost per customer, not by applause. And keep a second explanation in your pocket, because the numbers will tell you that something worked and they will never tell you why.
He would want you to doubt his book. He would mind far more if you never tested it.
ch.cap: An old adman writes his own life down

connects: Ogilvy built his own rules on this book and told the whole trade to read it seven times, so Ogilvy on Advertising is largely Hopkins with better tailoring.
Both books are about replacing confident opinion with scored, repeated tests and a tally you cannot argue your way out of.
The guarantee signed by the local chemist and the free sample are reciprocity and authority at work, found by trial and error forty years before Cialdini gave them names.
note: The life comes mainly from Hopkins's own My Life in Advertising of 1927, and every quotation here is taken from that book or from Scientific Advertising of 1923. It is a self written account produced decades after the events, so treat its figures as claims rather than records. Scholarly work on the Bissell company archives dates his Christmas breakthrough to 1890, cannot confirm all his sales numbers, and found evidence that his father deserted the family rather than died as he wrote, and his widely quoted salary of a hundred and eighty five thousand dollars rests chiefly on David Ogilvy's later testimony. The challenge to the Pepsodent story, that the film is a natural membrane brushing does not remove and that the habit was built by the tingle of citric acid and mint, comes from Charles Duhigg's The Power of Habit and the research behind it.
recall: What change did Hopkins make to Dr Shoop's guarantee, and why did it work?

He moved the signature from the distant manufacturer to the neighbourhood druggist, the person the customer actually handed money to. That borrowed trust the buyer already had rather than asking for trust in a stranger. He tested it first on a cough cure and reported enormous results.
How deep were the Schlitz artesian wells, and why was that fact persuasive?

Four thousand feet. The persuasive part is that the brewery stood on the shore of Lake Michigan, so sinking wells that deep looked almost absurdly unnecessary, which is precisely what made it proof of care. Hopkins said it helped him give purity a meaning.
Where did Schlitz stand before and after the campaign?

It was in fifth place when Hopkins began. By his own account it jumped to neck and neck with first place within a very few months, usually described as drawing level with Budweiser. He called it one of his greatest accomplishments.
What did Hopkins call the substance on teeth, and where did he find it?
He called it the film. He came across a reference to mucin plaques while reading dental textbooks, and built the whole Pepsodent campaign on the instruction to just run your tongue across your teeth.
Which single figure did he insist all conclusions rest on?

Cost per customer, or cost per dollar of sale. He wrote that mail order advertising is traced down to the fraction of a penny, and that almost any question can be answered, cheaply, quickly and finally, by a test campaign.
recap: Claude Hopkins was born in Michigan in 1866 into a house with a long line of preachers behind it and no money in it. Five services every Sunday, no walking for pleasure, nothing to read but the Bible and a Concordance. From nine years old he warmed schoolhouses before dawn, carried newspapers to sixty five homes and swept a church on Sundays, while his mother taught school and sold her own kindergarten books from door to door. He was being groomed for the ministry, and at eighteen he stood in a Chicago pulpit, with his mother watching, and said there was no hell fire and that Jonah and the whale would not survive examination. The congregation filed out in silence. Days later his mother told him he was no longer her son. He kept the preaching and threw away the believing. At the Bissell Carpet Sweeper Company he sold five thousand letters worth of carpet sweepers as the Queen of Christmas Presents and got a thousand orders back, and discovered that the post bag settles arguments. At Swift he built the largest cake in the world to sell a cooking fat that cost more than its rival, and a hundred and five thousand people climbed four flights of stairs to see it. In Racine he moved a patent medicine guarantee from a distant factory to the local chemist who would hand your money back, work he later said he could no longer approve of. For Schlitz he toured a brewery, found plate glass cooling rooms, bottles washed four times, wells sunk four thousand feet beside Lake Michigan and a mother yeast cell bred through twelve hundred experiments, put the dull details into print and moved the beer from fifth place to level with first. At Lord and Thomas he wrote food shot from guns, keyed his coupons so he knew which headline paid, and for Pepsodent told a nation to run its tongue across its teeth, taking toothpaste from seven houses in a hundred to sixty five. Then he retired and wrote it all down in twenty thousand words: advertising is salesmanship, no generality has any weight whatever, the best ads ask no one to buy, and almost any question can be answered cheaply, quickly and finally by a test. The warning sits inside the triumph. Later research says he misread why Pepsodent won, and his own memoir does not quite match the records. Measure everything, and stay suspicious of your explanation.
stories: The largest cake in the world

Chicago in the 1890s, and Hopkins has to sell a cooking fat that costs half a cent a pound more than its rival, to bakers who will not even sample it. A department store, Rothschild and Company, is about to open. I will build there, he tells them, the largest cake in the world, baked with Cotosuet instead of butter. In one week a hundred and five thousand people climbed four flights of stairs to look at it, and the police had to shut the doors to control the crowd. He never argued about the price. He gave people something to come and see.
The sermon that ended a career

Eighteen years old, a Chicago pulpit, his mother in the pews. This was a boy raised on five services every Sunday and no books but the Bible and a Concordance. He stood up and told the congregation there was no hell fire, and that the story of Jonah and the whale would not survive examination. He called it afterwards the most daring event of my life. Nobody shouted. The audience filed out in silence and not one person came to greet him. Days later, over lunch on Dearborn Street, his mother told him he was no longer her son.

Touring a Quaker mill with Albert Lasker, Hopkins watched grain being fired out of steel guns under pressure to puff it up. He had Wheat Berries renamed Puffed Wheat and wrote the line food shot from guns. The advertising trade thought it idiotic and one paper called it the theory of an imbecile, on the grounds that nobody eats ammunition. Puffed Wheat and Puffed Rice became the two most profitable cereals in America, with sales of both up three hundred per cent. The campaign was simply the dullest fact on the factory floor, said out loud.
take: Replace every superlative with something checkable
Hunt down trusted, expert and leading in your copy and swap each for a number, a process or a date you can evidence. Specifics persuade and they also keep you compliant.
The dull thing nobody has said is usually the advertisement
Every brewer filtered their beer; only Schlitz described it. Walk your own operation, write down the boring steps, and look for the one your competitors have never bothered to mention.
Key everything or you are guessing
Give every advert, keyword and channel a traceable code, and ask the source question at the start of the call, not the end. Judge it on cost per customer, never on cost per lead.
Reverse the risk with trust you have borrowed
Hopkins moved the guarantee from the distant manufacturer to the local chemist. Put your reassurance in the hands of whoever your customer already believes.
Offer service before you ask for the order
The best ads ask no one to buy. Lead with something useful on its own terms, then let the enquiry follow from gratitude rather than pressure.
A test ends the argument a meeting cannot
When two sensible people disagree about copy, run both versions, and agree the sample size and the decision rule before you look at the result.
Measurement tells you what worked, never why
He proved Pepsodent worked and still got the reason wrong. Always keep a rival explanation alive and design the next test to separate the two.
Write your numbers down at the time
His memoir does not match the records. Memory inflates, so log the figures the week they happen and let your later self be corrected by them.
title: The Preacher Who Counted the Collection
wiifm: You buy attention from Google, Bing and Facebook every day, and every pound of it is either working or quietly leaking. This is the man who first insisted that you could know which. He turned persuasion into arithmetic, with keyed coupons instead of opinions, and left behind a handful of rules that still decide whether your advertising pays: say something specific, offer service before you ask for the order, settle arguments with a test, and judge the lot on cost per customer. You also get the cautionary half, because he measured beautifully and still misread why his biggest winner won.
words: A medicine of doubtful value sold on extravagant claims, and by extension any pet scheme pushed as a cure for everything.
Hopkins spent six and a half years in Racine writing advertisements for nostrums, and later disowned that entire class of work.
Widely repeated and probably not true.
Several of the best anecdotes in his memoir, including some of the Bissell sales figures, look at least partly apocryphal beside the company's own records.
Based on observation and measurement rather than theory or opinion.
His real contribution was to make advertising empirical, settling arguments with keyed coupons instead of taste and seniority.
A word or slogan repeated so often inside a group that it signals membership while carrying no real meaning.
Pure had become a brewer's shibboleth, and Hopkins beat it by describing the filters, the deep wells and the twelve hundred yeast experiments.
Writing that treats its subject as a saint rather than as a person.
My Life in Advertising is part manual and part hagiography, with Hopkins serving as both the author and the saint.
